output.name: Mirske
output.myth:
Aun flew the Mirske over the Reach, and every winter he had come through alive he tied a knot in its tail. By his third spring the tail hung heavy with them, and he was proud. He laughed at the Gale.

Tavo heard the laughing. He came down off the Windward Reach like a dropped net and tore the kite from its string. Aun watched it climb with every knot still in its tail. Kiskan the Wind-Gull, seventeen degrees west, was first to chase it, and still cannot catch it.

Hesk, at the pole, counts the knots as they pass her, and she counts them still. Keret the Pole-Runner, flying up from the north, carries the count to her. Ennu says the Mirske flies over the Reach on windy nights, heavy and slow, and the children learn their numbers from it. When a grandmother dies, her family ties one more knot on a small kite and lets it go, so the count keeps going.

If you see the Mirske, do not count its knots out loud. Hesk will hear you and ask you to hold the string.
output.finding: Find Keret the Pole-Runner in the north, then look one hand-span straight south of it, where the Tally Kite hangs in the Windward Reach.
